St Neots crews shine during exciting Bumps week (Image: Supplied) The Men's Second Eight, coxed by club captain Christina Dunn, had an eventful week, racing twice on several evenings. The John Jenner Trophy, awarded to the club with the greatest overall improvement, was won by St Neots Rowing Club. Rowers secure bumps and silverware on River Cam (Image: Supplied) Club captain Christina Dunn said: "It has been many years since the club last lifted the John Jenner Trophy, making this year's success particularly special and a testament to the hard work, commitment, and determination of every athlete, coach, and volunteer involved." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman to abseil down 400ft tower for blood cancer charity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire woman is taking on a 400-foot abseil in a bold show of courage and hope. Brittany Mumford, from Brampton, will descend from the world’s tallest permanent abseil tower in support of Lymphoma Action. The event, called Don’t Look Down, takes place on Saturday, September 19, during Blood Cancer Awareness Month and marks the charity’s 40th anniversary. Ms Mumford said: "When people think of cancer, they don't often picture a healthy 27-year-old mum with an eight-week-old baby in her arms – me included. "When I was sitting at the hospital during my tests, feeding my baby, I thought, 'They're making a big mistake here – I'm fine!' "Then the words 'you have cancer' brought a harsh ending to my naivety." Ms Mumford was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma shortly after the birth of her second child. This September marks six years since she went into remission. She said: "Through Lymphoma Action, I found the support I really needed. "They helped me understand what I was going through and connected me with others who understood – people who knew the fear of waiting for scan results, the grief of losing your old life, the uncertainty of not knowing what comes next, and the hope of life after treatment." Ms Mumford said she hopes to raise funds and awareness for those affected by lymphoma, the most common type of blood cancer in the UK. Laura Thompson, challenge events fundraiser at Lymphoma Action, said: "We are so grateful to Brittany and her family for their support. "Our daredevil challenge would make Spiderman think twice, but every step taken down the tower by our brave abseil team will help us make sure no one faces lymphoma alone." Ms Mumford’s fundraising page can be found at justgiving.com/page/brittany-mumford-2.

Police were called to Huntingdonshire District Council's offices at Pathfinder House on April 14. Matthew Howson, 33, poured a can of lighter fluid on the lobby floor and lit it with a match. He then produced a Stanley knife from his pocket, before walking out the building, leaving a member of the public to extinguish the fire. Shortly afterwards, police were called to the former Fire Station in Huntingdon, after receiving a report that a man was refusing to leave the premises. At Peterborough Crown Court on Wednesday (19 August), Howson, of Grosvenor Yard, Newmarket, was jailed for one year and ten months. He admitted to arson, possessing a knife in a public place, and breaching a stalking protection order. The final charge relates to Howson failing to notify police about a change of address. DC Emily South, who investigated, said: "Howson's actions were extremely reckless and could have had serious consequences. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A firefighter who has been tackling a wildfire at a nature reserve in Cambridgeshire for the past 12 days said he saw "huge flames" and "200 foot trees" falling around him. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 and continues to smoulder away, burning up to six metres below the surface deep in the peat. Fire crews from across the country have been on site assisting Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. Holme Fen is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) due to the variety of wildlife, plants and fungi found across the 657 acres of landscape. The area of destruction caused by the fire extends to 95 acres. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) Crew Manager Jake Banks, from Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service, has been on the scene since the fire broke out. He said: "The conditions in the first seven to eight days were really, really hard. "Six to ten feet below ground, all the peat was well alight and recorded temperatures were up to 1,000 degrees." Exceptionally high temperatures and multiple heatwaves in Cambridgeshire this summer have only added to the pressure on fire crews. Crew Manager Jake Banks has been tackling the wildfire for 12 days (Image: Emily Stevens) Mr Banks said: "Obviously last week was very hot as well - 38 degrees some days here, with huge flames. "This area covers 60 football pitches in total, and then we have to battle that with all that heat and move all the hose around. "We also had the huge risk of 200 foot trees falling every couple of minutes around us, so it's been a long hard few weeks to be honest." The area of destruction covers 60 football pitches in total (Image: Emily Stevens) After nearly two weeks, there are no more open flames on site. Fire crews must now work to fell and clear out the trees in the area so they can begin to tackle the peat, which is still smouldering underground. The fire is deep in the peat, up to six metres below the surface (Image: Emily Stevens) Mr Banks said: "I think we've got a grasp on this now. "Now we're just here to support the machinery operators and make sure while they are moving all the fallen trees about, they are safe and there is no reignition anywhere." According to Assistant Chief Fire Officer Stuart Smith, it could be up to three or four weeks until the area has been cleared of trees and crews can start extinguishing the underground peat fire.

Four homes have been approved at a former kennels and cattery despite fears they could “open a floodgate” of development in the countryside. Plans for five houses at the site off Fenstanton Road near Hilton had been rejected in 2022 for being out of character for the countryside and being in an unsustainable location where residents would need to drive to access services. But the latest plans for four detached four-bedroom bungalows were recommended for approval by Huntingdonshire District Council’s planning officers. A design and access statement from Twenty Nine Architecture and Planning said the new plan “significantly reduced” the scale of the homes to a “modest single-storey form” more in line with the existing buildings on the site. The former Fields View Kennels and Cattery, which shut in 2020, would be demolished to make way for the homes. Hilton Parish Council still objected to the new plans and Cllr Peter Balicki spoke on its behalf to the council’s development management committee on Monday, August 17. He said that the last proposal was originally for seven homes before being revised down to six, and finally five. He said the parish council objected to these from “concern” that if homes were approved on the former agricultural site it would “open a floodgate of applications”. He said: “It just seems that you can turn the barrel of the kaleidoscope as many times as you like until it falls into place. “Now that we’ve gone from seven failed, six failed, five failed – we’ll let permission be given for four”. James Aldridge, of nearby Alpha Farms, said he was concerned that future residents of the homes could complain about his poultry farm – despite it being there first. He said: “Our farm is already here and is a working farm – there will naturally be noise, smells, dust, farm vehicles and muck movements. “If people move into these houses and then complain about these normal farming activities, could that lead to the council putting restrictions on our farm? “We want to know that our farm can continue to operate normally in the future.” The council’s planning officer said national planning policy states that existing sites “should not have unreasonable restrictions” placed on them as a result of new developments being approved nearby. An odour assessment also took place, which was not done for the previous application, and officers said they didn’t think odour or noise would negatively impact future residents. Cllr Alan Hunt, of St Neots Eatons, raised concerns that two parking spaces per home would not be enough and visitors would be forced to park on the road which could lead to a “real highway safety risk”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “From our visit to the site there was nowhere on the side of the road that I felt was actually safe for that kind of parking. “It’s a rural road, it’s a 60mph limit and the visibility is not brilliant.” Cllr Jon Neish said that even though cycle parking would be provided at the homes, they’ll still be largely car dependent as they would be “in the middle of nowhere”. The Conservative councillor said: “I wouldn’t want to cycle down there – I was lucky I was on a motorbike at the time, so it was two wheels, but it had an engine. “I just think it’s a little bit awkward myself and I’ve not been convinced that it actually is the right use for this.” Cllr Tom Sanderson said that, since the highway authority didn’t object to the plans, it would be “very difficult” for them to refuse based on parking or road safety concerns. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “If this went to appeal, the fact is we are in tilted balance – that dreaded phrase. “I think if this were to be rejected, it would be very difficult to justify doing so at appeal.” The application was passed by a single vote with five voting in favour, four against and four abstaining.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We tried the lunch menu at newly refurbished Prezzo Italian in Peterborough
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: I was very excited to be invited to Prezzo in Peterborough to try out their lunch menu after their recent refurbishment - and it did not disappoint. Firstly, the restaurant's decor is gorgeous. A member of staff told me they had undergone a complete revamp around six weeks ago to give the space a fresh feel, as before it was apparently a little dark. That certainly isn't a problem anymore; the space feels bright, airy and colourful with modern wood finishes and bold prints on the walls. Prezzo's interior (Image: Emily Stevens) Prezzo's bar (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister and I were seated near the front of the restaurant by the window, but the space is deceivingly large and extends back a long way. There is even a garden space at the back for outdoor dining. Prezzo's outdoor dining space (Image: Emily Stevens) We started off with drinks and both went for one of their homemade coolers. I tried the Wild Strawberry Lemonade, which was delicious, very refreshing and perfect for the unrelenting hot weather we have had this summer. My sister had a Citrus Cooler, which she loved as well and said it was very well presented. Wild Strawberry Lemonade and Citrus Cooler (Image: Emily Stevens) Next we shared the Tomato Bruschetta and some olives to start. We both agreed that the bruschetta was the highlight of the meal; the bread was perfectly crisp but still soft inside and the tomatoes on top were elevated so well by the fresh pesto and balsamic glaze. My sister remarked that the pesto was especially flavourful and we both enjoyed the olives too which came dressed with olive oil and garlic. Olives and Tomato Bruschetta (Image: Emily Stevens) For the main course, I tried one of the specials: the Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti. The pork meatballs were delicious; they were very well seasoned and had a melting cheese centre which I really enjoyed. The pasta tasted freshly made as well, and everything was brought together with a rich tomato sauce that had a bit of a kick from the nduja. Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister was slightly overwhelmed by the size of her vegetable calzone - you definitely get your money's worth with this dish! She liked the marinara dipping sauce it came with and said the dough was excellent; it was finished with a bit of garlic butter and parmesan. However, she did say the vegetable and cheese filling could have been slightly more flavourful. Vegetable Calzone (Image: Emily Stevens) Despite nearly clearing all our plates so far, we decided we had to make room for dessert. I went for the Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie which was the ideal way to finish. The meringue was perfectly fluffy and complemented the tart lemon filling and buttery pastry very well. Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie (Image: Emily Stevens) However, I actually preferred my sister's tiramisu which was deliciously creamy and rich. It was a bit of a sweeter take on a classic tiramisu and wasn't overly alcoholic which we enjoyed. Tiramisu (Image: Emily Stevens) Both of us had a great time at Peterborough's Prezzo and will definitely be back. The menu had a huge variety of dishes, from classic Italian pizzas and pastas to different burgers and salads, so there is definitely something for everyone. Expect large portion sizes for main courses though, so be sure to leave room for dessert.

Her family has grown significantly, and she now has 12 grandchildren, 18 great-grandchildren, and eight great-great-grandchildren. Throughout her life, Mrs Smith has been known for her hard work and love for activities such as horse riding, dog walking, dancing, dressmaking, gardening, and swimming. The data also shows the RSPCA received 40 per cent all reports of cruelty towards wild birds during the summer months last year. While there is no single explanation for the overall rise, the RSPCA believes a range of factors may contribute to deliberate attacks on wildlife. These can include deliberate misuse of catapults and air weapons, copycat behaviour, greater exposure to harmful online content, and a lack of understanding about animal welfare. Mike Scargill, wildlife partnerships manager for the RSPCA said: "We are deeply concerned by the number of reports involving deliberate cruelty towards wild birds. "Day after day, our frontline officers and animal centres see the sickening consequences of weapons being used on animals - causing awful suffering, severe injuries and often leading to death. "These figures are likely to represent only a fraction of the true scale of the problem because a lot of cruelty goes unseen and unreported. Concerns had been raised about the 74 hectare site off Low Fen Drove Way in Horningsea’s impact on nearby Grade-II listed Biggin Abbey. The proposal is also next to a site where the sewage treatment works in Cambridge was set to be relocated – but the future of this is unclear after the government withdrew funding. The application was recommended for approval by council officers who said it would be “temporary and low scale” and considered the land to be grey belt – a site considered to make only a limited contribution to the green belt. John Hughes, from the National Trust, said that “significant opportunities” were missed in the application to improve biodiversity and nature recovery. He said: “With a close proximity to Cambridge and other local populations, an opportunity to better connect with people and nature has been missed along with the varied social benefits it would provide.” Although the scheme “substantially exceeds” the requirement for biodiversity net gain, Mr Hughes said this was largely through “passive measures” like the conversion of arable land to grassland. He said: “For a development of this scale on green belt land we would have expected a more ambitious and integrated approach to nature recovery.” An agent for the developer said the scheme had “significant benefits” and would support “both local and national renewable energy and decarbonisation targets”. She said: “South Cambridgeshire Council declared a climate emergency in 2019 and this year’s climate and nature strategy committed to a 50 per cent reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050 for area wide emissions. “This is well evident in the climate conditions we’re seeing across the UK and Europe this week.” Councillor Anna Bradnam, speaking as ward councillor for Milton and Waterbeach, said that although the scheme is described as temporary, “40 years is half a lifetime”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I respect the officer’s view but regret that the green belt protections which used to be so strong have been eroded by this concept of grey belt. “I believe this development would have a degrading and industrialising impact on the countryside in this area – how can 74 hectares of glass and metal for 40 years be considered a minor adverse impact?” Cllr Vivien Biggs, of Swavesey, said that the development couldn’t be argued to enhance the area, but they had to consider balance. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I think we have to be pragmatic, and obviously anybody having something like this in their back yard is not going to be particularly happy. “It’s not beautiful, but we also know we don’t own the view unless we own the land.” Cllr Heather Williams, of The Mordens, also said that planning was about “trade-offs” and there will never be a “perfect solution”. The Conservative councillor said: “There’s merit for it in its objectives but, in my view, there’s a lot of policies it comes into conflict with. “I think we need more renewable energy and I 100 per cent understand why farming communities are looking to things like solar in the current situation – but there are alternative places.” The solar farm was approved with four voting in favour and one against. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Acclaimed theatre producer becomes patron of Hunts creative organisation
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share An acclaimed theatre producer has been named as the newest patron of a creative organisation. Rachel Tackley MBE will take up the patronage at Neotists CIC, a champion of the creative industries in St Neots and the wider Huntingdonshire area, bringing extensive experience from a prominent career in UK theatre. Ms Tackley is currently interim creative director and co-chief executive of the Arts Theatre Cambridge, where she has led the venue’s reopening and renewal following major redevelopment. Richard Slade, CEO and co-founder of Neotists CIC, said: "We are thrilled to welcome Rachel as a patron of Neotists CIC. "Her achievements in theatre, from Chichester and Riverside Studios to her leadership at the Arts Theatre Cambridge, speak to exactly the kind of ambition and quality we want to see reflected in our own community. "Having someone of Rachel’s standing and experience backing our work is a real vote of confidence in what we are building in St Neots." Alongside her current roles, Ms Tackley is a producer for Heartaches Ltd and is involved in the upcoming production Sherlock Holmes and the 12 Days of Christmas, set to open at Alexandra Palace this December. She has also contributed to Arts Council England’s new Incentivising Touring Fund. Previous senior positions include executive director of Chichester Festival Theatre, director of English Touring Theatre, and creative director of Riverside Studios. Ms Tackley is chair of Bretforton Theatrebarn in the Cotswolds and a director of Lyric Hammersmith Productions. She also serves on the advisory board of the Cambridge School of Creative Industries at Anglia Ruskin University. Rachel, who lives locally with her family, brings a wealth of national and international experience to Neotists as it continues to grow its support for creative professionals across the district. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A Cambridgeshire man who sent explicit messages and images to what he mistakenly thought was a 14-year-old girl has been jailed. Iain Fleming, 53, from Millfield in Peterborough, began communicating with a decoy account run by an online child abuse activity group in March last year. Despite the “girl” telling Fleming she was only 14 several times, he continued sexual communication with her and sent explicit images of himself. Police were contacted by the child activist group, and officers swiftly arrested Fleming at his Peterborough home. After seizing his mobile phone, it was also revealed Fleming had contacted what was believed to be a 15-year-old girl. He continued with explicit conversations, telling her she had "a beautiful body" and that "he wanted to kiss her all over", according to Cambridgeshire Police At Peterborough Crown Court on Friday (7 August), Fleming, of Millfield, Peterborough, was jailed for three years and two months. He admitted two counts of attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child, and one count of attempting to incite a girl to engage in sexual activity. DC Lloyd Davis, who investigated, said: "Fleming clearly poses a significant risk to children. "Despite the ‘girl’ in this case being a decoy account, Fleming still attempted to prey on and groom what he believed was a child. "This kind of sexual exploitation can have devastating effects on a child’s development, mental health and self-esteem that continue into adulthood, so I am pleased he is now behind bars for his crimes." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots Town FC mascot raises £650 in Mascot Gold Cup
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A football mascot’s race nearly ended in glory—until a tumble just shy of the finish line. Rowley the Warthog, St Neots Town FC’s mascot and the alter ego of club stalwart Harry Fisher, took part in the Mascot Gold Cup at Wetherby Racecourse, raising nearly £650 for East Anglia’s Children’s Hospices (EACH) and Ronald McDonald House UK. Mr Fisher said: "My pride was a little bruised, but the most important thing was that we managed to raise money for two amazing charities that mean a lot to many people at St Neots Town FC. "It was a fantastic experience, lining up against so many other mascots from across the country. "I turned up quite relaxed, but my competitive nature got the better of me, and as soon as the race started, I was in it to win it." St Neots Town FC mascot Rowley the Warthog (Image: Supplied) Mr Fisher, who wore the warthog costume for the race, was in second place and closing in on a silver medal before he tripped just before the finish line. He said: "I was flying and looked certain to secure a respectable second-place finish. "Then, only yards from the finish line, I somehow managed to trip over one of my huge trotters and lost several places, as well as my costume head." The funds raised will be split between EACH and Ronald McDonald House UK. A representative from EACH will collect the donation at an upcoming home game at the Premier Plus Stadium. Mr Fisher said: "With the new season having just started, the exercise was great preparation for our home games when I’ll be running around meeting fans. "Last season was Rowley’s first as St Neots Town FC’s mascot. "There are so many great volunteers at the club, but, surprisingly, not many jumped at the opportunity to put on the warthog outfit." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Stray dog's 'ear attached to neck' in one of worst cases of matting'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An investigation has been launched after a two-year-old stray dog was found with "suspected deliberate injuries" hidden beneath its matted fur. Peanut, a Shih Tzu-Lhasa Apso cross was found in Ross Street, Cambridge, on July 2, before he was taken to Woodgreen Pets Charity. When he arrived, concerns were immediately raised about his condition, especially his fur. Peanut's coat was so severely matter that one of his ears became attached to his neck, preventing him from turning his head properly. Woodgreen's veterinary team safely clipped and removed the layers of matted fur. However, they discovered concealed beneath his coat a series of vertical wounds running along his body from his back to his belly. Although the injuries were healing, the pattern and nature of the wounds led the veterinary team to suspect they had been deliberately inflicted. Following his treatment, Woodgreen carried out an investigation into his owner's history. Peanut was found with several unusual wounds believed to have been caused deliberately (Image: RSPCA) This included scanning Peanut's microchip, investigating his previous ownership history and sharing information with the RSPCA. Emma Lyons, veterinary surgeon at Woodgreen Pets Charity, said: "Peanut's condition was one of the worst cases of matting we've seen. "His fur had become so overgrown and tightly knotted that one of his ears was effectively attached to his neck, severely restricting his movement and undoubtedly causing him significant discomfort. "Once we removed the matted coat, we discovered several unusual wounds along one side of his body. "While we cannot say with certainty how they were caused, their appearance is highly concerning and not something we would typically expect to see as the result of an accident. "Our priority was to relieve Peanut's pain, begin treatment and ensure he received the care he so desperately needed." RSPCA animal rescue officer Maya Thakrar, who is investigating the circumstances surrounding Peanut's injuries, said: "The injuries found on Peanut are extremely unusual. Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen (Image: RSPCA) "Although they were already healing by the time he arrived at Woodgreen, they would have caused him considerable pain. "We are working to establish exactly what happened to Peanut and are particularly keen to speak to anyone who recognises him or knows who cared for him before he was found. "Even the smallest piece of information could prove vital to our investigation." Microchip data suggest Peanut was rehomed approximately six months ago, and the RSPCA is keen to trace the person who took ownership of him at that time. Despite everything he has endured, Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen. Martina Cohen, dogs team leader at Woodgreen Pets Charity said: "Peanut's resilience has amazed everyone who has cared for him. "Our team feels lucky to have had the chance to watch him grow in confidence during his time with us, and his cheeky personality and zest for life is shining through more and more each day. "It's heartbreaking to think about what he's been through, but thanks to the dedication of our veterinary and care teams, he now has the chance of the happy future every dog deserves."
